passage:
Subject: LEOPARD near my school!!
Naveen bhai,
You won't believe this. A leopard was seen behind our school in Kothrud on Monday night. It's totally true. Siddhesh's cousin's friend works as a guard there and he saw it at 2:14 a.m., drinking from the tank near the basketball court. He even said it had a torn left ear and walked with a limp. Who makes up a torn ear? That's how I know it's real.
Ammi says leopards almost never come into our part of the city, and the forest office hasn't said anything. But the detail about the ear is so exact. Nobody would invent that.
I'm not going near the back gate till they catch it.
Write back soon,
Farhan

qa.q: What detail about the leopard makes Farhan so sure the story is true?
qa.a: It had a torn left ear and walked with a limp.

qa.q: Why does the torn ear convince Farhan more than what Ammi said?
qa.a: The exact detail makes the story feel like something a real witness saw, while 'leopards almost never come here' is a plain fact that feels weaker, even though it matters more.

qa.q: What could Farhan do before believing and spreading the story?
qa.a: Farhan could start from how rare leopard visits are in that area, notice the story came through three people, and check whether the forest office or the school has said anything.

qa.q: How might Naveen read this email?
qa.a: Naveen might notice the 'cousin's friend' chain and the missing official news, and gently ask Farhan how often leopards really come there.

grounding: It shows a teenager trusting a vivid, second-hand report of a rare event over how seldom such events happen.

passage: Everyone at college still calls me Forward-Yamini, so here's why I stopped forwarding stuff. In Class 9, Vaibhav was absent for four days, and a girl from the next section told us he'd been expelled. Her mum works in the school office, she said, and she described everything: the principal slamming a blue file shut, Vaibhav's father walking out into the rain without his umbrella. I believed every word. I even messaged three people. Then on Friday Vaibhav walked in with a chess trophy. He'd been at a district tournament. Honestly, in ten years at that school I'd heard of maybe one expulsion, ever. But the blue file and the umbrella felt so real that I never counted. Now when a story has lots of juicy details, I ask how often that thing actually happens.

qa.q: Where had Vaibhav really been for four days?
qa.a: He'd been at a district tournament, and he walked in with a chess trophy.

qa.q: Why did Yamini believe the expulsion story so completely?
qa.a: The blue file and the umbrella in the rain made it feel like an eyewitness account, so Yamini never stopped to count how rare expulsions were at that school.

qa.q: What habit did Yamini build, and why does it work?
qa.a: Yamini now asks how often a thing actually happens whenever a story is full of juicy details, which puts the plain odds back beside the vivid story.

qa.q: What was it like for Vaibhav to be the subject of this rumour?
qa.a: Vaibhav came back proud of a trophy only to find people had been told he was expelled, which could feel confusing and hurtful. 😔

grounding: It shows a teenager believing a detailed rumour of a rare expulsion while ignoring how seldom expulsions happen.

passage: My younger sister Lakshmi stopped revising on Tuesday evening. I noticed because her chemistry notes stayed shut on the bed and she was humming. When I asked, she held out her phone: a forwarded message saying the Class 10 board exams were cancelled for our state. It had a circular number, a round stamp, even a signature in blue ink. "Look, it's official, Sangeeta akka," she said. I don't know what was going on in her head, but she seemed relieved, almost giddy. I said I couldn't remember board exams ever being cancelled like that, not once in all my school years. She shrugged. "But the stamp." We checked the board's own website together. Nothing. She went quiet, then opened the chemistry notes again, slowly.

qa.q: What did the message on Lakshmi's phone say?
qa.a: It said the Class 10 board exams were cancelled for their state.

qa.q: Why did the message feel believable to Lakshmi?
qa.a: The circular number, the round stamp and the blue signature made it look official, and she was relieved at the idea, so how rare cancellations are never crossed her mind.

qa.q: Which step worked here, and why?
qa.a: Checking the board's own website together worked, because it tested the vivid message against a reliable source instead of arguing about the stamp.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta see her sister's behaviour?
qa.a: Sangeeta sees only the outside, the shut notes, the humming and the relief, and says she doesn't know what was in Lakshmi's head.

grounding: It shows a teenager trusting an official-looking message about a very rare event because its details seem reliable.

passage:
Monday: Gargi, fifteen, read the forwarded message three times. "Scientists predict a strong earthquake in our city this Thursday, 3:12 pm." There was a map with red circles, the name of a professor, even a reference number. "Look how exact it is," she told Neelam. "Nobody makes up 3:12."
Thursday: At three, Gargi was sitting in the school ground with her bag packed and her shoes on. Neelam sat beside her. "How many times has an earthquake ever been warned to the minute?" Neelam asked. Gargi didn't answer. At 3:12 a crow landed on the goalpost. Nothing else happened.
Saturday: Gargi searched for the professor's name. She found the same message, word for word, sent around three other cities in past years. "It sounded so real," she said.

qa.q: What exact time did the forwarded message give for the earthquake?
qa.a: 3:12 pm on Thursday.

qa.q: Why did the message feel so trustworthy to Gargi?
qa.a: The map, the professor's name, the reference number and the exact minute all felt like proof, so the vivid detail pushed aside how rarely such a warning ever comes true.

qa.q: What turning point changed Gargi's view, and what could she do earlier next time?
qa.a: Finding the same message sent around other cities in past years; next time she could first ask how often such events really happen and check where the message came from before packing her bag.

qa.q: What was Thursday afternoon like for Neelam, sitting beside Gargi?
qa.a: Neelam seemed calm and a bit doubtful, choosing to stay with Gargi and ask a gentle question instead of mocking her fear.

grounding: It shows a teenager sure a rare event would happen because a detailed report seemed reliable, ignoring how uncommon it is.

passage:
Thomas, you're sure your friend's story is true because he gave you so many details? Sit. Let Noor aunty tell you about the night a film star came to Kottayam.
I was sixteen. My best friend Leela swore she had seen him at Joseph's bakery at eleven at night. White car, blue shirt, he ordered plum cake and paid with a thousand-rupee note. She even knew his driver's name. I believed every word. I told my whole class, my cousins, the milkman.
Now think. How often did a film star come to a small-town bakery at night? Almost never. And how often did someone who looked a bit like one pass through? Every wedding season.
It was a groom from Pala, going home after his reception. Leela's details were all correct. Only the man was wrong.

qa.q: What did Leela say the man ordered at the bakery?
qa.a: Leela said he ordered plum cake and paid with a thousand-rupee note.

qa.q: Why did young Noor believe Leela so completely?
qa.a: The white car, the blue shirt, the cake and even the driver's name made the story feel certain, so Noor forgot how rarely a film star would ever turn up at a small-town bakery.

qa.q: What question could have helped young Noor before telling the whole class?
qa.a: Noor could have asked how often a film star really visits such a bakery compared with how often a lookalike passes through, which would have made the groom far more likely.

qa.q: How might Thomas look at the friend's detailed story after hearing this?
qa.a: Thomas may realise that lots of correct details don't prove the rare part is true, and start asking how common the event is before believing it.

grounding: It shows a teenager convinced a rare event happened because a vivid, detailed report seemed reliable, while ignoring how uncommon it was.

passage: Manoj, sixteen, refused to cycle to the tuition class in the next village. "A leopard was seen in Patil's sugarcane," he told his cousin Santosh. "Ganesh bhau saw it himself, at dusk. Big yellow eyes, a long tail, and it was dragging something off towards the goat shed." Santosh pointed out that nobody in the village had seen a leopard in forty years. "Forty years doesn't matter. Ganesh bhau doesn't lie, and he described the spots!" Manoj said. Santosh shrugged. "Honest people can still see a big jungle cat in the dark." By evening the sarpanch had called the forest office. The ranger found only small pawprints and a torn feed sack, and Patil's goats were all safe in their shed. Manoj still took the long road for a week.

qa.q: Who did Manoj say had seen the leopard?
qa.a: Manoj said Ganesh bhau saw it himself, at dusk.

qa.q: Why did the report feel so convincing to Manoj?
qa.a: Manoj felt scared and certain because the report came from someone he trusts and was full of vivid details like the yellow eyes and the spots, which felt stronger than forty quiet years.

qa.q: What could Manoj ask himself the next time a frightening report spreads?
qa.a: He could ask how often this has really happened nearby and whether an honest person might have mistaken something smaller in poor light, then wait for someone who checks, like the forest office.

qa.q: How does Santosh see the leopard story?
qa.a: Santosh stays calm and weighs the forty years without a leopard more than the dramatic description.

grounding: Shows a teenager trusting a vivid report of a rare leopard sighting over how seldom such sightings actually happen.

passage: In Valencia, the whole of class 3B buzzed on Monday: Señora Ortiz had not come in, and a substitute sat at her desk. By lunch, Sofia was sure. "She's been fired," she told her friends. "Javier's cousin works in the office. He heard shouting on Friday, saw her carrying a box to her car, and the head closed the blinds." It sounded exactly like a film. Javier, stirring a yogurt, said quietly, "Teachers get sick all the time. Nobody's been fired here since we started." "But the box, Javier! The blinds!" Sofia wrote a long message to the class group before the bell. On Wednesday Señora Ortiz was back, pale and hoarse, a scarf around her neck. The box had held old exam papers for recycling. Sofia deleted her message and avoided the teacher's eyes.

qa.q: What had the box carried by Señora Ortiz actually held?
qa.a: The box had held old exam papers for recycling.

qa.q: Why did the firing story feel true to Sofia?
qa.a: Sofia felt thrilled and certain because the shouting, the box and the closed blinds made a vivid picture that seemed more real than the plain fact that teachers often get sick.

qa.q: What could Sofia have done before writing to the class group?
qa.a: She could have asked how often teachers are fired compared with how often they are simply ill, and waited a day or two for real news.

qa.q: How might Señora Ortiz feel if she saw Sofia's message?
qa.a: She might feel hurt and embarrassed that her class believed she had been fired while she was only ill.

grounding: Shows a teenager treating a detailed second-hand report as proof of a rare event while overlooking how common the ordinary explanation is.

passage: The notice board outside the hostel mess said nothing, but Nitin, the mess monitor, said plenty. "A Class 9 girl collapsed after lunch. Her lips went blue, the nurse came running, they took her away in the van." Dolma, fifteen, pushed her tray away. "It's the dal. It tasted sour today, I knew it." Her roommate reminded her that the mess had served the same dal every Tuesday for three years without one sick child. "But her lips went blue," Dolma said. "You don't make that up." She ate biscuits from her trunk that night and lay awake listening for other girls being sick. At morning assembly the nurse explained that the girl had skipped breakfast before a long run and was already fine. Dolma quietly went back to the dal.

qa.q: What did Dolma blame for the girl's collapse?
qa.a: Dolma blamed the dal, which she said tasted sour.

qa.q: Why did the collapse story make Dolma feel sure the food was bad?
qa.a: Dolma felt frightened and sure because the blue lips and the rushing nurse made the story vivid, so three years of safe Tuesday dal felt less real than one dramatic detail.

qa.q: What could Dolma do the next time a scary story spreads in the hostel?
qa.a: She could ask how often the mess food has actually made anyone ill and check with the nurse or the warden before changing what she eats.

qa.q: How does Dolma's roommate see the dal?
qa.a: The roommate trusts the long record of the same dal every Tuesday with no one falling sick, so one story isn't enough to be scared.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager believing a rare food-poisoning story because of vivid details and ignoring years of meals that caused no harm.

passage:
Dear Gurleen,
You won't believe what happened this week. On Monday someone posted a photo in our colony group: a leopard near Block C, at night. The photo was blurry, but the man who posted it is a retired army officer, very serious, so everyone believed him. So did I. I stopped walking to tuition alone, and I made Mummy drive me.
On Thursday Papa asked, "How often do leopards come into a city colony?" I said, well, it happens. He showed me that in thirty years, there had been no leopard anywhere in our district. "And big stray dogs?" Every night.
On Friday the forest department checked the camera near Block C. It was the fat yellow dog from the dhaba.
I'm walking again. And I'm embarrassed.
Raghav

qa.q: Who posted the leopard photo in the colony group?
qa.a: A retired army officer, very serious.

qa.q: Why did Raghav believe the leopard story?
qa.a: Raghav felt scared and trusted it because a serious retired officer posted it, forgetting how rare leopards in a city colony are.

qa.q: What question from Papa helped, and why?
qa.a: "How often do leopards come into a city colony?" It made Raghav start from how rare the event is before trusting a blurry report.

qa.q: How might the retired officer feel after the camera check?
qa.a: He might feel embarrassed, having frightened the colony with a blurry photo of a stray dog.

grounding: A teenager's letter shows Raghav believing a rare leopard sighting because the report seemed reliable, ignoring how uncommon it is.

passage: Chaitanya, you remember the physics paper panic? Let me tell you from my side. So, I'm Farhan, and on Sunday night a senior, a topper, very sure of himself, told me the board paper had leaked. He even said which questions. I believed him completely. He's never wrong about exams. I spent the whole night studying only those five questions. But think about it. How many times in, like, twenty years has our state board paper actually leaked? Once, maybe? And how many times do rumours like this go around? Every single exam. The topper just sounded reliable. I forgot how rare a real leak is. In the morning, none of those questions came. Not one. I had skipped two whole chapters for a rumour. My father said, "Next time, ask how often it's really true."

qa.q: How many questions did the senior say had leaked?
qa.a: Five questions.

qa.q: Why did Farhan believe the senior completely?
qa.a: Farhan felt trusting and anxious, because the senior was a topper who sounded sure, so the rare event of a real leak seemed likely.

qa.q: What does Farhan's father suggest, and why is it good advice?
qa.a: To ask how often such a thing is really true, since real leaks are very rare while rumours come every exam.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya remember the physics paper panic?
qa.a: Chaitanya may remember the stress of that night too, and see Farhan's mistake as common among students.

grounding: A teenager explains believing a rumoured exam leak because a topper sounded reliable, ignoring how rare real leaks are.

passage:
Tuesday. A red warning flashed on Devika's phone: "Your device is infected! 3 viruses found. Call this number now." It had an official-looking shield and her phone company's colours. Devika's heart pounded. "My phone's been hacked," she told Zeenat at lunch. "Look, it even knows my phone model."
Wednesday. Devika hadn't called the number, but she was scared to use her phone. Zeenat asked her brother, who worked in IT. He said real hacks of ordinary phones like hers were rare, and fake warnings like this were everywhere, every day.
Thursday. Devika showed the screen to her father. He closed the browser, and the warning disappeared. He showed her how to block pop-ups. "It looked so real," Devika said. "That's the point," he said. "The trick is common. The hack isn't."

qa.q: What did the red warning on Devika's phone say?
qa.a: Your device is infected! 3 viruses found. Call this number now.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when the warning flashed?
qa.a: She felt frightened, heart pounding, sure her phone had been hacked because the warning looked official.

qa.q: What helped Devika, and what could she do next time?
qa.a: Asking Zeenat's brother and then her father, who explained fake warnings are common; next time she can remember how rare real hacks are before panicking.

qa.q: How does Devika's father see the warning?
qa.a: He sees it as a common trick, which is why he closes it calmly and teaches her to block pop-ups.

grounding: Shows a teenager sure her phone was hacked because a warning looked reliable, ignoring how rare real hacks are and how common fakes are.

passage:
Lavanya, you believed that forward about the bridge collapsing because it had photos? Let me tell you about my leopard.
I was fifteen, in Nashik. One morning a boy in my class said he'd seen a leopard behind the school canteen. He described it perfectly: the spots, the yellow eyes, a torn ear. He was a serious boy, top of the class. I believed every word, and by lunch I'd told half the school.
My grandfather asked me, "When was the last leopard seen in our part of town?" Nobody could remember one, not in fifty years. "And how many big yellow dogs live behind that canteen?" Three, at least.
I was annoyed with him. The story was so detailed.
That evening the watchman found the leopard: a big spotted street dog with a torn ear. I, Shankar, never lived it down.

qa.q: Where did the boy say he had seen the leopard?
qa.a: The boy said he'd seen a leopard behind the school canteen.

qa.q: Why did Shankar believe the leopard story so quickly?
qa.a: Shankar felt excited and trusting, because the detailed description and the serious boy made the report seem reliable, so the rarity of leopards didn't seem to matter.

qa.q: Which question in the story could have changed things, and why?
qa.a: The grandfather's questions about the last leopard seen and the number of dogs behind the canteen, because they compare a very rare event with a very common one.

qa.q: How might the classmate who reported the leopard have felt when the watchman found the dog?
qa.a: The classmate probably felt embarrassed, having honestly believed the sighting and then seen it turn out to be a spotted street dog.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a teenage belief in a rare leopard sighting because a report seemed reliable, ignoring how uncommon leopards were.

passage:
It was 10 p.m., the night before the board chemistry exam, and the power had just gone off in the whole lane. Arnab sat by the inverter lamp, scrolling a class group.
LEAKED PAPER, the message said. A blurry photo of a question sheet, a seal half visible, and a senior "from a reliable source" promising that question 4 was on electrolysis.
"It's real," Arnab told Rajni, who was revising at the other end of the mat. "Look at the seal. And he's a topper."
"How many times has the board paper actually leaked in the last ten years?" Rajni asked, not looking up.
"I don't know. Once? Never? But this one has details!"
"Every fake one has details. That's how they spread."
Arnab stared at the blurry seal, then at his untouched organic chapter. With two hours of battery left, he closed the group and opened the textbook.

qa.q: What did the message promise question 4 would be on?
qa.a: The message promised that question 4 was on electrolysis.

qa.q: Why did the leaked paper feel real to Arnab?
qa.a: Arnab felt hopeful and convinced by the seal and the topper's name, so the vivid details outweighed how rarely real leaks happen.

qa.q: Which choice helped Arnab under time pressure?
qa.a: Closing the group and using the last two hours of battery to revise the organic chapter, instead of betting on a rare leak.

qa.q: How does Rajni see the leaked paper?
qa.a: Rajni is unimpressed, since fake leaks always come with details, and keeps revising.

grounding: Shows a teenager believing a rare exam leak because the report looked reliable and detailed, while forgetting how uncommon real leaks are.

passage:
The message reached Pradeep's phone at the Lucknow bus stop: a white van, two men in masks, a child taken from Aminabad market at 5:40 yesterday. Share to warn everyone!
Pradeep's heart thumped. The details were so exact: the time, the colour, the masks. He forwarded it to four groups and told his mother he wasn't going to the market for his tuition books.
Nirmala, his cousin, read it at dinner. "Pradeep, in all your years in this city, how many children do you actually know of who were taken like this?"
"None. But this one has a time and everything."
"Made-up stories can have times." She searched the police page on her phone. "Here. The police say this exact message goes around every few months. Fake."
Pradeep felt his face go warm. He opened the four groups and typed: Sorry, this was fake.

qa.q: At what time did the message say the child was taken?
qa.a: The message said a child was taken from Aminabad market at 5:40 yesterday.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep believe the message and forward it?
qa.a: Pradeep felt frightened, and the exact time, colour and masks made the story feel reliable, so he never stopped to think how rare such cases are.

qa.q: What could Pradeep do before forwarding a scary message next time?
qa.a: Pradeep could ask how often such things really happen and check a trusted source, like the police page Nirmala found, before sharing.

qa.q: How might Pradeep's mother have felt when he refused to go to the market?
qa.a: She may have felt worried and confused, suddenly hearing that Pradeep was too scared to go out for books.

grounding: Shows a teenager believing a vivid rumour of a rare kidnapping because its details seemed reliable, ignoring how uncommon such events are.

passage:
"Nandini, it's confirmed. The maths board paper has leaked."
"Confirmed by who?"
"My cousin's friend's uncle works at the printing press. He saw the envelope open. He even said the paper was blue, with a crease on the second page."
"Kalyani, how many times has the board paper actually leaked?"
"Once? Years ago?"
"And how many times has someone said it leaked?"
Kalyani paused, twirling her dandiya stick; the Navratri music was already starting in the school ground. "Every year, I guess."
"So which is more likely: this is the one rare real leak, or the usual rumour with extra details?"
"But the crease! Nobody makes up a crease."
"People make up creases all the time."
"Fine. But I'm still skipping chapter nine."
"Then I'm revising it twice, just for you."

qa.q: Where does Kalyani say the uncle works?
qa.a: At the printing press.

qa.q: Why does Kalyani feel sure the paper leaked?
qa.a: The vivid details, like the blue paper and the crease, make the report feel reliable, so Kalyani feels convinced and excited, forgetting how rare real leaks are.

qa.q: What would you advise Kalyani about chapter nine?
qa.a: Keep revising it, since real leaks are rare while rumours come every year, and check any such news with a teacher.

qa.q: How does Nandini judge the rumour?
qa.a: Nandini compares how seldom real leaks happen with how often rumours appear every year, so the extra details don't impress her.

grounding: Shows a teenager sure a rare exam leak happened because a detailed report seemed reliable, ignoring how uncommon real leaks are.
